sections.title: 1. Purpose and place in the outline

blocks.text: The outline sets Grade 3's focus as multiplication and division fact mastery, and an introduction to fractions (§3B). Its exit standard is math-fact automaticity: "the single best predictor of later algebra success" (§3B, §5).

Arithmetic is one of two courses that sit in both cadences (§7). The facts need spacing, so a short drill lives in the daily core. The instruction doesn't, so lessons and practice live in the weekly queue. This plan keeps the two parts separate and says how they fit together.
Mastery over exposure (§1): a child moves on when a skill is automatic, not when the calendar says so. The platform tracks mastery per skill, not per week (§8).

blocks.text: Why this order. Multiplication meaning comes in Term 1, as the first facts are drilled. Division meaning waits until Term 3, once most multiplication facts are known, and division facts are drilled in Term 4 as the reverse of facts already automatic. Fractions come in Term 5, when sharing and division are secure, because a fraction is a kind of division.
The outline's exit standard for arithmetic is math-fact automaticity (§5, Grade 3). This plan defines it as:
Oral: answers any multiplication fact through 10 × 10, and its division partner, within about three seconds, without counting on fingers or skip-counting under the breath.
Written: 60 mixed multiplication and division facts in 3 minutes, with 95% accuracy (57 or more correct).
Addition and subtraction facts to 20 remain automatic.

The check comes in week 36. A child who doesn't meet it continues the daily drill in Grade 4 on the families still missing, before Grade 4's long division begins. Long division is built on these facts, and starting it without them is the most common reason children come to dislike math.

Daily drill, Day 5 fact check: 20 facts from the week's family, written. 18 of 20 within two minutes is mastery for that family. Below that, the family repeats next week before a new family is added. The facts aren't going anywhere; the next family can wait.
"Tricky facts" card: facts missed on any check go on a small card the child keeps. They join Day 2 and Day 4 every week until answered instantly three times in a row.
Speed sheets are for the child's own progress. Record the scores, but don't grade them.

Term check (week 6 of each term): about 20 problems on the term's concepts, plus a word problem section. 16 of 20 is mastery. Below it, the next term opens with a review week on the concepts missed (§8: pause rather than accumulate a deficit).
Auto-graded drill for facts suits the platform well (§8). The term checks and word problems stay parent-marked, because the working matters as much as the answer.
Show the work. From Term 1, word problems are written with a short number sentence and a labeled answer ("12 pennies", not "12").

items.label: Lesson — Rounding to tens and hundreds

blocks.text: Rounding finds the nearest "friendly" number. Draw a number line from 40 to 50 and mark 47: it's closer to 50.
The rule: look at the digit just to the right of the place you're rounding to. 5 or more, round up; 4 or less, round down.
Models: 47 to the nearest ten is 50. 365 to the nearest ten is 370. 438 to the nearest hundred is 400. 2,950 to the nearest hundred is 3,000.
Why it matters: rounding gives a quick estimate, used from next week to check addition and subtraction answers.

blocks.text: A polygon is a closed, flat shape with straight sides. A circle is not a polygon (no straight sides); an open shape is not a polygon (not closed).
Names by sides: triangle (3), quadrilateral (4), pentagon (5), hexagon (6), octagon (8).
Vertices are the corners where sides meet. A polygon has as many vertices as sides.
Special quadrilaterals: a rectangle has 4 right-angle corners; a square is a rectangle with all 4 sides equal. So every square is a rectangle, but not every rectangle is a square.
Go on a shape hunt around the house: a window (rectangle), a stop sign in a picture (octagon), a honeycomb (hexagons).

A line goes on forever in both directions. A line segment has two endpoints. A ray has one endpoint and goes on forever the other way.
A right angle is a square corner, like the corner of a book. Test any angle with the corner of an index card: if it fits exactly, it's a right angle.
Parallel lines run side by side and never meet, like railroad tracks. Perpendicular lines meet at a right angle, like a plus sign.

A shape is symmetrical if a line can split it into two halves that match exactly, like the two halves of a butterfly. That line is the line of symmetry.
The fold test: cut out a shape, fold it along a line. If the halves match exactly, it's a line of symmetry.
Some shapes have more than one: a rectangle has 2, a square has 4, a circle has as many as you like.
Letters: A, H, M, T, U, V, W, X, Y have lines of symmetry; F, G, J, L, N, R don't.

blocks.text: A graph shows numbers as a picture, so they can be compared at a glance.
Pictographs use a symbol for a number of things. Always read the key: if one tree picture means 2 trees, then 3 pictures mean 6 trees.
Bar graphs use bars. Read the number at the top of each bar from the scale on the side. The scale may count by 2s, 5s or 10s.
